ARTICLE B9: PERSONNEL LIMITATIONS  
Advisory Committee: SAC  
Governance: F1 Commission / WMSC 
B9.1 General Provisions 
B9.1.1 All persons concerned in any way with an entered F1  Car or present in any other capacity 
whatsoever in the paddock, Pit Lane , or track during a Competition must always wear an 
appropriate pass. No pass may be issued or used other than with the agreement of the FIA. A pass 
may be used only by the person and for the purpose for which it was issued. 
B9.2 Operational Personnel  
B9.2.1 At each Competition during the period beginning twenty-nine (29) hours before the scheduled start 
of FP1 and ending two (2) hours after the start of the Race , each Competitor may not have more 
than a total of sixty (60) “Operational Personnel” who are associated in any way with the operation 
of the F1 Cars within the confines of the circuit.  
However, during the period starting forty-five (45) minutes before the start of the first formation lap 
until fifteen (15) minutes after the scheduled start of the Race the number of such Operational 
Personnel is unlimited. 
B9.2.2 For the avoidance of doubt Race drivers and staff whose duties are solely connected with 
hospitality, marketing, media, security or driving trucks to or from the Competition are not 
considered Operational Personnel.  
B9.3 Trainee Personnel  
B9.3.1 In addition to the sixty (60) personnel described in Article B9.2.1, each Competitor will be permitted 
sixteen (16) individual exceptions during a Championship  for “Trainee Personnel”. However, no 
individual trainee may attend more than three (3) Competitions in this capacity. 
B9.4 Declaration of Personnel  
B9.4.1 A list of all operational, trainee, shared, and employee guest personnel must be submitted to the 
FIA prior to the start of Restricted Period One using the DMS and the official template provided by 
the FIA. 
Amendments to the submitted list of all operational, trainee , shared , and employee guest  
personnel after the start of Restricted Period One shall be permitted at the sole discretion of the 
FIA. 
A list of all personnel exempt from the provisions of Article B9.2 or B9.3 who have been working on 
behalf of the Competitor within the restricted areas of the circuit during the Competition must be 
submitted to the FIA prior to the end of the Competition,  using the DMS and the official template 
provided by the FIA.  For the avoidance of doubt the restricted areas of the circuit include the 
paddock, the competitors Designated Garage Area, the pit lane or the signalling area. 
B9.5 Restricted Period(s)  
B9.5.1 At each Competition, with the exception of the provisions of Article B9.5.2, Operational Personnel 
and Trainee  Personnel, as defined in Articles B9. 2.1 and B9.3.1 , are not permitted within the 
confines of the circuit during the Restricted Periods.

B10.1 Media Activities 
B10.1.1 Day before on track running  
a. Up to six drivers will be selected to participate in official media and promotional activities (as 
defined by the Media Delegate) for a maximum duration of one (1) hour during a two (2) hour 
period, commencing 23 hours prior to the scheduled start of FP1.  
i. Any driver not taking part in an official FIA Press Conference (as designated by the Media 
Delegate) must take part in a separate written media and broadcast session organised by 
their team. 
ii. These separate media sessions will take place in time slots defined by the Media Delegate 
and must not be held at the same time as any official FIA Press Conference. 
b. Within a one (1) hour period commencing 20 hours and 30 minutes prior to the scheduled start 
of FP1, six (6) drivers must be available for fan engagement activities for a maximum period of 
thirty (30) minutes each (this window includes the time required to travel to and return from the

to specific event requirements; any changes will be communicated to the relevant 
Competitors no later than four (4) weeks in advance.

Competition (requirements and format as defined by the Media Delegate, in conjunction with 
the Commercial Rights Holder). This summary document must be provided no later than 
twenty-three (23) hours prior to the scheduled start of FP1.

surfaces. If only one F1 Car will carry the major aerodynamic and bodywork components 
and assemblies that have not been run at a previous Competition or TCC and are intended 
to be run at the Competition, this F1 Car must be the one displayed to media.

emergency services detailed in Supplement 1 of Appendix H to the ISC are followed.

“Alternative Format Competition” (or “AFC”) is any Competition where a Sprint is scheduled. 
“Current Car” (or “CC”) is defined as a car which was designed and constructed in order to comply with the 
FIA F1 Regulations of the 2026 or subsequent Championships. No Competitor may sell or make available any 
such Current Car to any third party without the prior authorisation of the FIA. 
“Demonstration Event” (or “DE”) shall be defined as an event in which a Competitor participates purely for 
marketing or demonstration purposes. 
“Document Management System” (or “ DMS”) is the FIA provided document management and exchange 
system used as the primary means of document exchange with Competitors during a Competition. 
“Fast Lane”: The Pit Lane will be divided into two lanes, the lane closest to the pit wall will be designated the 
Fast Lane and may be no more than 3.5 metres wide. 
“Historic Car” (or “HC”) is defined as a car which was designed and constructed in order to comply with the 
regulations in force during the years preceding those referred in the definition of a Previous Car. 
“Inner Lane”: The Pit Lane will be divided into two lanes, the lane closest to the garages will be designated 
the Inner lane. 
“Lap Time Classified Session” (or “LTCS”) is any track running session during which the classification of the 
session is determined based upon the time taken by a driver to complete a single lap. Lap  Time Classified 
Sessions include, but are not limited to, free practice sessions, the sprint qualifying session and the qualifying 
session. 
“Mule Car” (or “MC”) is defined as a car which was designed and constructed in order to comply with the 
Section C of the FIA F1 Regulations or with the technical regulations of any of the four (4) calendar years falling 
immediately prior to the calendar year of the Championship, but suitably modified for the purpose of providing 
the Tyre Supplier with a means of track testing of its future products or for providing the FIA with a means of 
testing components or systems for a future Championship. No Competitor may sell or make available any 
such Mule Car to any third party without the prior authorisation of the FIA. 
“Official Messaging System” (or “OMS”) is the FIA official messaging system that will be used as a means of 
real-time or near real -time communication to all Competitor s during a  Competition. Unless otherwise 
specifically defined, where in these FIA F1 Regulations where it is stated that a pre-determined message will 
be sent to all Competitors, or that all Competitors will be notified or informed of specific information during a 
competition, this will be done using the Official Messaging System. 
“Pit Entry Road”, unless otherwise defined by the Race Director, means the section of track leading to the Pit 
Lane, between the first safety car line and the beginning of the Pit Lane. 
“Pit Exit Road”, unless otherwise defined by the Race Director, means the section of track from the end of 
the Pit Lane  leading to the track, between the end of the Pit Lane  and the second safety car line, will be 
designated the Pit Exit Road.

1. BRAKES 
 1.1 Brake friction material may be removed, measured, de-glazed and refitted 
 1.2 The brake system may be bled.

2.1 In accordance with Article C3.10.10, adjustment of the position, not controlled by the FIA Standard 
ECU, of the Front Wing Profiles. No parts may be added, removed or replaced.  
 2.2 Bodywork (excluding radiators and heat exchangers) may be removed. 
 
2.3 Bodywork components may be inspected with the use of NDT methods, provided no disassembly 
takes place. 
 2.4 Cosmetic changes may be made to the bodywork and tape may be added. 
 2.5 Any part of the car may be cleaned.  
 2.6 Bodywork fixings and cable ties (consumable fasteners) may be replaced. 
 
2.7 
Any bodywork component may be repaired where the damage is patched, bonded, or fixed together.

replacement components or sub-components may be used.

items, provided the original components stay in vision of the scrutineer and are refitted once pitstop 
practice is completed.

specification of a car, all competitors will be notified (via the official messaging system) with the message 
“CHANGE IN CLIMATIC CONDITIONS”. From th is point onwards until the start of the subsequent sprint 
session or race changes may be made to: 
 3.1 Components specified in Articles C3.14.4 and C3.15.5. 
 3.2 Power unit and / or gearbox cooling bodywork that lies within RV -BODY-REAR and / or RV-RBW-EC 
reference volumes as defined in Appendix C2: Regulation Volumes. 
 3.3 
The settings of any bypass valves or flow restrictors used within the liquid part(s) of the cooling 
system(s) may also be adjusted, for the sole purpose of adjusting power unit and / or gearbox 
cooling. 
 3.4 The addition or removal of the Driver Cooling Scoop described in Article C3.7.6.

the mirrors, seat belts and pedals may only be carried out with the specific permission of the 
Technical Delegate. 
 4.2 Should ambient temperature change significantly, Competitors will be requested (via the official 
messaging system) to change the head padding required by Article C12.6.1.

APPENDIX B4: PODIUM CEREMONY 
Advisory Committee: SAC  
Governance: F1 Commission / WMSC 
At each Event the procedure for the Podium Ceremony is detailed below. 
1. MASTER OF CEREMONIES 
A master of ceremonies will be appointed by the FIA to conduct and take responsibility for the entire 
podium ceremony. 
2. PODIUM 
a. ROSTRUM AND DAIS 
The dimensions of the dais must follow those found in the FIA graphic design manual. 
The distance between the edge of the winner's dais and the retaining barrier of the podium should 
be a minimum of 120cm to provide a walkway. 
The place where each person presenting a trophy should stand must be marked on the floor of the 
podium. 
Trophies must be laid out on a single table on one side of the podium. The champagne must be on 
the dais. 
b. FLAGS 
Olympic Games style "flat flags" should be used. There must be a minimum space of 50cm behind 
the podium structure for the flag men. 
c. FLOOR 
The podium and steps should be covered in green or dark blue carpet. 
3. ANTHEMS 
a. The national anthem of the winning driver and winning constructor will be played. The 
Nationalities of the constructors and drivers will be notified to the organiser by the FIA and will 
accord with Article 9.5.2 of the ISC. 
b. A suitable sound system should be installed to ensure that national anthems, (initiated by the 
master of ceremonies) are clearly heard with an audio link to the TV broadcast. 
c. When the champagne shower begins, music should be played. This should not start until the 
presenters have left the podium. 
d. A commentary of the podium ceremony should be broadcast to the general public from the 
platform erected for the TV cameras. 
4. TROPHIES 
Only 4 trophies will be presented during the podium ceremony: 
a. Winning driver. 
b. A representative of the winning constructor. 
c. Second driver.

The height of the trophies shall be: 
h. Winner's and constructor's trophies - no less than 50cm and no more than 65cm high. 
i. Second and third drivers' trophies - no less than 35cm and no more than 45cm high. 
The maximum weight per trophy must not exceed 5kg. Trophies must be of a design that is capable 
of being handled and transported without damage. 
5. SCENARIO 
a. Only three persons should be on the podium to present the trophies. In exceptional 
circumstances, the master of ceremonies may increase this to four. 
b. No police, bodyguards or persons not authorised by the master of ceremonies are allowed on 
the podium. 
c. The master of ceremonies will inform the TV and public address commentator of the names of 
the persons presenting the trophies. 
d. The master of ceremonies must be on the side of the podium where the trophies are located. 
The persons presenting the trophies will be on the other side. The master of ceremonies will 
hand the trophies to those presenting them. 
6. TELEVISION 
The ideal position for the TV camera is immediately opposite the podium and at the same height. 
Under no circumstances must there be a TV camera man on the podium. 
7. PARC FERMÉ 
The parc fermé must be positioned as close as possible to the podium, preferably immediately 
below, with direct access. 
As soon as all the F1  Cars have crossed the Line, a course car must go round the track to collect 
any driver who has finished in the first three but is stranded on the circuit. 
The drivers must not be delayed in the parc fermé. One person, nominated by the master of 
ceremonies and in radio contact with them, will be responsible for moving the drivers from the parc 
fermé to the podium without delay. Only persons authorised by the master of ceremonies may 
make contact with the drivers before the end of the TV unilateral interviews. 
8. UNILATERAL ROOM 
The unilateral room must be adjacent to the podium. The master of ceremonies will see that the 
drivers proceed there immediately after the podium ceremony. The room should be suitably 
ventilated (or air conditioned if the temperature is above 25°C).

documents.title: Australian GP — Car 12 (unsafe release)
documents.text:
2026 AUSTRALIAN GRAND PRIX
06 - 08 March 2026
From The Stewards
To The Team Manager,
Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team
Document 42
Date 07 March 2026
Time 19:26
The Stewards, having received a report from the Race Director, summoned (document 37) and
heard from the team representative, have considered the following matter and determine the
following:
No / Driver 12 - Kimi Antonelli
Competitor Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team
Time 17:00
Session Qualifying
Fact Car 12 was released from its garage in an unsafe condition.
Infringement Breach of Article B1.6.2 b) i) of the FIA F1 Regulations.
Decision The Competitor (Mercedes-AMG Petronas F1 Team) is fined €7,500.
Reason The Stewards heard from the team representative of Car 12 (Kimi Antonelli) and
reviewed video, team radio and in-car video evidence.
Car 12 (Antonelli) was released from its garage during the session with a duct cooling
fan still attached on the right side of the car. The fan assembly disconnected from the
duct of Car 12 as it negotiated Turn 1, split apart and one section of it bounced off
the track onto the gravel at the exit. Another section of the fan assembly dislodged
onto the track at Turn 2 and was later struck by the front wing and tyre of another car
causing debris to be strewn over the track, damage to the front wing of the other car
and the session had to be red flagged to remove the debris.
The Team explained that an incident in an earlier session in which Car 12 had
sustained significant damage meant that the division of labour within the Team had to
be changed to repair the damage within a short time frame. Usually, a separate team
member would have responsibility for inserting and removing each fan but the need to
address legacy issues from the earlier incident during the session meant that the
team member responsible for the fan on that side of the car was occupied on another
task and the removal of the fan before the car was released from the garage was
missed. 
The Team (and the Driver) were unaware that the fan had not been removed until the
incident was noted by Race Control.
The Stewards determine that because Car 12 left its garage with a piece of
equipment still attached, it was released in an unsafe condition and the Stewards
impose a fine on the Competitor accordingly.
 
 

The Stewards
Competitors are reminded that they have the right to appeal certain decisions of the
Stewards, in accordance with Article 15 of the FIA International Sporting Code and
Chapter 5 of the FIA Judicial and Disciplinary Rules, within the applicable time limits.
 
Decisions of the Stewards are taken independently of the FIA and are based solely
on the relevant regulations, guidelines and evidence presented.
 
Nish Shetty Mathieu Remmerie
Pedro Lamy Matthew Selley

documents.title: British GP — Car 10 (impeding)
documents.text:
2026 BRITISH GRAND PRIX
03 - 05 July 2026
From The Stewards
To The Team Manager,
BWT Alpine F1 Team
Document 60
Date 04 July 2026
Time 19:01
The Stewards, having received a report from the Race Director, summoned (documents 51 & 52)
and heard from the driver of Car 10 and the team representatives, have considered the following
matter and determine the following:
No / Driver 10 - Pierre Gasly
Competitor BWT Alpine F1 Team
Time 16:09
Session Qualifying
Fact Car 10 unnecessarily impeded Car 18 at Turn 15 at 16:09.
Infringement Breach of Article B4.1.1 of the FIA F1 Regulations.
Decision Drop of 3 grid positions for the next Race in which the driver participates.
Reason The Stewards heard from the driver of Car 10 (Pierre Gasly), the team
representatives and reviewed video, telemetry, team radio and in-car video evidence.
STR was on a timed lap in Q1. GAS was on an in lap and, on the approach to Turn
15, remained on the racing line at a slow speed, requiring STR to move off line in
order to pass.
GAS explained that he had no functioning radio at the time, that he had been
attempting radio checks and that he expected another driver (ANT), to remain behind
him rather than overtake, as he understood ANT not to be on a timed lap. The team
representative pointed out that there was no radio warning to GAS because of a
technical issue with FOM equipment, which was confirmed by FOM.
The Stewards accepted that these were unfortunate circumstances and took into
account that the driver was left without the usual radio warning from the team. The
team representative of STR also confirmed that, in his view, the circumstances were
unfortunate.
However, the absence of a radio warning does not remove the driver’s responsibility
to avoid impeding another car. GAS remained at a slow speed on the racing line and
the evidence showed that the driver had information available to him, including the
dashboard display, to appreciate STR was approaching on a timed lap.
In those circumstances, the Stewards determined that GAS unnecessarily impeded
STR and therefore impose the standard penalty of a 3 grid position drop.
Competitors are reminded that they have the right to appeal certain decisions of the
Stewards, in accordance with Article 15 of the FIA International Sporting Code and
Chapter 5 of the FIA Judicial and Disciplinary Rules, within the applicable time limits.
Decisions of the Stewards are taken independently of the FIA and are based solely
on the relevant regulations, guidelines and evidence presented.

The Stewards

Mathieu Remmerie Pedro Lamy
Richard Norbury

documents.title: Canadian GP — Car 30 (article c9.3)
documents.text:
2026 CANADIAN GRAND PRIX
22 - 24 May 2026
From The Stewards
To The Team Manager,
Visa Cash App Racing Bulls F1 Team
Document 26
Date 22 May 2026
Time 17:18
The Stewards, having received a report from the Race Director, have considered the following
matter and determine the following:
No / Driver 30 - Liam Lawson
Competitor Visa Cash App Racing Bulls F1 Team
Time 15:00
Session Free Practice 1
Fact The CDS did not function when the car stopped on the track.
Infringement Breach of Article C9.3 of the FIA F1 Regulations.
Decision The competitor (Visa Cash App Racing Bulls F1 Team) is fined €30,000, €20,000 of
which is suspended for a period of 12 months subject to no further breach of this
regulation by the Competitor, for either of its cars. 
Reason The Stewards heard from the driver of Car 30 (Liam Lawson), team representatives,
the FIA Technical Delegate and FIA Electronics Engineer and reviewed telemetry and
in-car video evidence.
The team’s engineer explained how the CDS system worked.  It was noted that the
system on this car performs two roles – the one for which is it primarily intended,
namely to release the clutch when the car is stopped and the engine is not working,
and the other relates to the anti-stall system.  In this case, a ruptured joint caused a
hydraulic leak, which caused the car to stop.  The CDS, when activated by the
marshal, then failed to release the clutch and hence the car could not be moved.
This is a serious matter.  It resulted in the session being red-flagged. Had the system
worked as intended by the regulations, the incident could have been dealt with swiftly
via deployment of the Virtual Safety Car.
The Stewards note the concern of the FIA Technical Delegate, over the dual purpose
of the CDS on this car.  The Technical Delegate advised that the team had, in 2025,
been warned about the CDS system design for its cars.
The Driver noted that there were two issues of concern that he wished to draw to the
attention of the Stewards, namely that contrary to his instructions and common
practice, the marshals attempted to push the car when it was stationary, and that the
marshal who attempted to activate the CDS was trying to press a button on the on-
board camera rather than the CDS button.  This indicates to the Stewards that further
training in this area is required, notwithstanding the fact that the FIA distributes a very
clear document addressing this action. (ref “FIA Single Seater Recovery
Specifications”).  We note that it is obvious that the distribution of such a document,
although well detailed, probably needs supplementing with some form of practical
training by the organisers.

The Stewards
Competitors are reminded that they have the right to appeal certain decisions of the
Stewards, in accordance with Article 15 of the FIA International Sporting Code and
Chapter 5 of the FIA Judicial and Disciplinary Rules, within the applicable time limits.
Decisions of the Stewards are taken independently of the FIA and are based solely
on the relevant regulations, guidelines and evidence presented.
Garry Connelly Tanja Geilhausen
Pedro Lamy Marcel Demers

documents.title: Austin
documents.text:
Circuit of the Americas (Austin) — Circuit Notes

COTA was purpose-built for F1 with a mix of corner styles deliberately inspired by other famous circuits (its Turn 1 uphill esses draw comparisons to Silverstone's Maggotts-Becketts, and its infield section nods to several classic European tracks). Overtaking difficulty is moderate (≈0.35) — the long back straight into Turn 12 is a reliable passing zone, similar in concept to Austin's fellow modern-build permanent circuits like Shanghai and Bahrain.

Tyre degradation is moderate (≈3/5), safety car frequency and DNF rate are both fairly average for the calendar (≈0.3 and ≈0.1), and rain is a real if secondary factor (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.15) given the circuit's Texas autumn date, which can bring sudden storms. Pit-lane loss time (≈21s) sits near the calendar median, making strategy calculations here comparatively "textbook" relative to outlier circuits like Montréal (very short pit loss) or Monza (very long pit loss).

COTA is a useful calendar "baseline" circuit in modeling terms — none of its reference-table values are extreme outliers in either direction, so it's a reasonable circuit to compare a more unusual track's characteristics against when explaining why a prediction differs from the calendar median.

documents.title: Bahrain Sakhir
documents.text:
Bahrain International Circuit (Sakhir) — Circuit Notes

Bahrain International Circuit is a permanent desert facility, not a street circuit, and it sits at the easy end of the overtaking-difficulty spectrum (overtaking_difficulty ≈ 0.25, tied for the lowest in the calendar alongside Spa). Its long straights (up to ~1,100m) feed into wide, heavy-braking corners with multiple lines through the apex, which is exactly the geometry that makes passing straightforward relative to a street track. This is a big part of why grid position tends to matter less here than at a track like Monaco — a driver who qualifies poorly still has real chances to recover position during the race.

The abrasive desert surface and sustained high-speed cornering load make this one of the higher tyre-degradation circuits on the calendar (tyre_degradation_level ≈ 4/5), so strategy and stint management carry real weight in the finishing order, not just one-lap pace. Safety car interventions are moderate (≈0.3 frequency) — the run-off areas are generous by modern standards, which keeps incident-triggered cautions from being as constant as on a street track, but the fast corners and high tyre wear still produce enough incidents to matter. Rain is essentially a non-factor here (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.0) given the desert climate, so weather-driven strategy swings that show up at wetter European rounds don't apply at Bahrain.

Because the season often opens here, Bahrain also tends to be a track where pre-season form is least tested by in-season development — form features reflect the prior year's competitive order more directly than at later rounds.

documents.title: Baku
documents.text:
Baku City Circuit — Circuit Notes

Baku combines a tight, twisting old-city section with the longest straight on the calendar (≈2,200m) running alongside the Caspian Sea — one of the most unusual layout combinations in Formula 1. That long straight, feeding into a hard-braking zone, is a genuine overtaking opportunity, which keeps overtaking_difficulty at a moderate level (≈0.35) despite how unforgiving the narrow old-town section is if a driver gets it wrong.

Baku has the highest safety_car_frequency in the entire reference table (≈0.7) and one of the highest DNF rates (≈0.18) — the combination of very high top speed on the straight and wall-lined, low-run-off corners in the castle section means incidents here are frequent and tend to require full safety car neutralization rather than resolving under local yellow flags. The circuit's braking-zone count is low (only 4) relative to its length, which is part of why it doesn't behave like a typical technical street track — most of the lap is either flat-out or a single hard braking event, rather than the constant direction changes of a track like Singapore.

Tyre degradation is on the lower side (≈2/5), since the layout doesn't put sustained lateral load through the tyres the way a flowing permanent circuit does — most of the stress here is longitudinal, from the very hard braking zones rather than cornering load.

documents.title: Barcelona
documents.text:
Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya — Circuit Notes

Barcelona was, for decades, F1's primary pre-season testing venue, so teams historically know this track's characteristics better than almost anywhere else on the calendar — a fact that shows up in how predictable the competitive order tends to be here relative to a novel street circuit. It's a permanent circuit with a demanding mix of high-speed and medium-speed corners, and it's rated among the higher end of the tyre-degradation scale (≈4/5) — the long, high-load corners (particularly the final sector's sustained cornering) put significant lateral stress through the tyres over a race distance.

Overtaking difficulty is moderate-to-high (≈0.65) — there is a DRS zone into Turn 1, but the technical middle sector offers few genuine passing chances, so track position gained in the first few corners tends to hold. Safety car frequency is the lowest in the entire reference table (≈0.2), and DNF rate is similarly low (≈0.1) — this is a circuit with generous run-off and a layout that punishes pace more than it punishes small mistakes, so races here tend to run green from start to finish more often than almost anywhere else on the calendar.

Because degradation is high but overtaking is hard, strategy (undercut/overcut timing) tends to matter more here than outright overtaking on-track — a well-timed pit stop can gain track position in a way that a wheel-to-wheel move often can't.

documents.title: Budapest
documents.text:
Hungaroring (Budapest) — Circuit Notes

The Hungaroring is a tight, twisty permanent circuit often described as "Monaco without the walls" — there's more run-off than a street circuit, but the layout offers almost no long straights and a constant sequence of medium-speed corners that make following (let alone passing) another car extremely difficult. Overtaking difficulty is rated near the top of the calendar (≈0.8, just behind Zandvoort and well behind only Monaco) — this is one of the clearest examples of a permanent circuit behaving like a street track in terms of how much grid position dictates the finishing order.

Because the layout is so technical and low-speed relative to the rest of the calendar, DNF rate is among the lowest in the reference table (≈0.08) — there simply aren't many high-consequence corners to crash out of, races here tend to be processional and low-drama by F1 standards. Tyre degradation is moderate (≈3/5), and rain is a real if not dominant factor (≈0.1) given the mid-summer Central European date.

Because overtaking is so hard here, qualifying performance is an especially strong predictor of finishing position — a driver who has a bad Saturday at the Hungaroring has fewer realistic paths back through the field than almost anywhere else on the calendar besides Monaco.

documents.title: Imola
documents.text:
Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari (Imola) — Circuit Notes

Imola is a fast, old-school permanent circuit with very few genuine overtaking zones — most of the lap is flowing, high-commitment corners taken in quick succession, with only a couple of real braking-zone passing opportunities (notably into Tamburello and the Variante Alta chicane). That's why overtaking_difficulty is rated high here (≈0.75), closer to Hungaroring and Zandvoort than to a power circuit like Monza. Grid position and clean qualifying pace matter disproportionately at tracks like this, because a driver who gets stuck behind a slower car often has nowhere to pass until the car ahead makes a mistake.

Tyre degradation is moderate-to-high (≈3/5) given the sustained high-speed direction changes, and rain shows up here more than at the desert/Gulf rounds (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.15) — Imola sits in a part of Europe with genuinely unpredictable spring weather, and a wet or drying track at this circuit tends to scramble the grid more than usual precisely because overtaking is already hard in the dry, so drivers who gain track position in mixed conditions are much harder to repass once it dries.

Safety car frequency (≈0.5) and DNF rate (≈0.15) are both on the higher side for a permanent (non-street) circuit — the lack of run-off in several places (this remains one of the more old-fashioned tracks on the calendar) means an off-track excursion is more likely to end a car's race than at a modern Tilke-designed layout.

documents.title: Jeddah
documents.text:
Jeddah Corniche Circuit — Circuit Notes

Jeddah is one of the fastest street circuits ever built for Formula 1 — narrow, wall-lined, and taken at very high average speed despite being a temporary/semi-permanent street layout (is_street_circuit = 1). That combination is precisely why it carries one of the highest safety-car frequencies in the calendar (safety_car_frequency ≈ 0.6): walls punish even small errors, and at the speeds this track is run, an off-line moment easily becomes a barrier contact rather than a spun car that rejoins under its own power. DNF rate is correspondingly elevated (≈0.15).

Overtaking difficulty sits in the middle of the calendar (≈0.55) — there are genuine passing zones into the long back-straight braking area, but the blind, high-speed corners elsewhere on the lap punish a driver who commits to a move without a clear picture of what's ahead, so overtakes are riskier to attempt than the number alone suggests. Tyre degradation is comparatively low (≈2/5) for a track run at such high average speed, since the layout favours flowing, low-slip-angle corners over the sustained lateral loading that chews through tyres elsewhere.

Because Jeddah is a street track, track evolution across the weekend is significant — the surface rubbers in a lot between first practice and qualifying, which is part of why practice pace here is a noisier predictor of race pace than at a permanent circuit with a more stable surface.

documents.title: Las Vegas
documents.text:
Las Vegas Strip Circuit — Circuit Notes

Las Vegas joined the calendar in 2023 as a purpose-built street circuit run at night down the middle of the Strip, past the Bellagio fountains and the Sphere. It has the second-longest straight in the reference table (≈1,900m, behind only Baku), which creates a genuine, high-speed overtaking opportunity, keeping overtaking_difficulty at a moderate level (≈0.35) despite being a street circuit — most street tracks (Monaco, Singapore, Jeddah) skew harder to pass at than this.

The circuit is run very late at night in cold desert-adjacent conditions (Vegas in November), which is atypical for F1 — track temperatures are unusually low for the sport, and tyre_degradation_level is rated on the lower side (≈2/5) partly as a result, since cold track temperatures reduce the aggressive degradation seen at hotter rounds. Safety car frequency is moderate (≈0.4), and rain is effectively a non-factor given the desert climate (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.0).

As one of the newest circuits in the reference table, Las Vegas has comparatively little accumulated historical race data behind it relative to a long-established venue — its row is a real, current-generation street circuit rather than a rough inaugural-year estimate, but the model still has fewer prior seasons to draw driver/team track-form history from here than at, say, Monza or Silverstone.

documents.title: Le Castellet
documents.text:
Circuit Paul Ricard (Le Castellet) — Circuit Notes

Paul Ricard hosted the French Grand Prix through 2022 before dropping off the calendar — it's included in the reference table with a valid range ending in 2022, so it's a good example of the table's era-keying handling a circuit's departure rather than treating it as a permanent fixture. It's a wide, modern permanent circuit with the distinctive asphalt run-off "safety zones" instead of gravel traps, and one of the longer straights outside Baku/Las Vegas (≈1,800m) feeding the Mistral straight braking zone.

Overtaking difficulty was moderate-to-high (≈0.6) — the wide track surface actually made side-by-side racing easier in some sections than the number alone suggests, but a genuinely quick middle sector limited how often drivers found themselves close enough to attempt a pass. The circuit had the lowest DNF rate (≈0.08) and one of the lowest safety-car frequencies (≈0.1) in the whole reference table — the asphalt run-off areas meant an off-track excursion very rarely ended a car's race or triggered a caution, since a driver could simply rejoin without contact.

Because it's no longer on the calendar, this circuit's data only ever appears as historical training rows (2022 and earlier) — the model will never need to produce a live prediction here, but the historical rows remain useful, leakage-safe training signal for the general relationship between circuit layout and outcome.

documents.title: Lusail Qatar
documents.text:
Lusail International Circuit (Qatar) — Circuit Notes

Lusail is a fast, flowing desert circuit originally built for motorcycle racing before being adapted for F1, with a long sequence of high-speed corners that place unusually high demand on tyres — tyre_degradation_level is rated at the top of the scale (≈4/5), among the highest in the reference table alongside Bahrain, Barcelona, Silverstone, and Suzuka. Overtaking difficulty is moderate (≈0.55) — there are passing opportunities, but the high-speed nature of most corners means a driver needs a real pace advantage, not just a slipstream, to make a move stick.

Safety car and DNF rates are both fairly typical for the calendar (≈0.3 and ≈0.1 respectively), and rain is effectively a non-factor given the Gulf desert climate (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.0), similar to Bahrain and Jeddah. As a floodlit night race on a circuit built for two-wheeled racing, track temperature management (rather than rain) is the more significant weather-adjacent variable here — track temp tends to be more stable and cooler at night than an equivalent daytime desert race, which affects tyre degradation modeling more than any rain-probability feature would.

Given the combination of high degradation and moderate overtaking difficulty, race outcomes here tend to be shaped as much by who manages their tyres best across a long stint as by grid position alone.

documents.title: Madrid
documents.text:
Madrid Street Circuit (IFEMA / MADRING) — Circuit Notes

Madrid joined the F1 calendar in 2026 as a new street circuit built around the IFEMA convention center complex, combining permanent-facility sections with temporary street segments — a hybrid layout style similar in spirit to Miami and Las Vegas rather than a pure downtown street track like Monaco or Baku. Its reference-table row is explicitly flagged as an inaugural-circuit estimate: with zero prior seasons of real race data at the time it was added, its proxy values (overtaking_difficulty ≈ 0.6, safety_car_frequency ≈ 0.5, pit_lane_loss_time ≈ 21s, tyre_degradation_level ≈ 3/5) are reasoned from public layout facts and comparison to similar hybrid circuits, not derived from historical results the way an established circuit's row is.

As is standard for the reference table, this row should be revisited and refined once real race data accumulates — a circuit's actual overtaking and safety-car behavior often differs from pre-race estimates in ways that only show up once cars have genuinely raced there under representative conditions (tyre wear patterns, real overtaking attempts, real incident history). Until then, any prediction or explanation involving Madrid should be understood as resting on a rougher circuit-characteristics foundation than a prediction for a well-established venue like Silverstone or Monza.

Being a street circuit (is_street_circuit = 1) with an urban setting, Madrid also inherits the general street-circuit pattern seen elsewhere in this dataset: comparatively pronounced track evolution across a race weekend as the surface rubbers in, and a moderate-to-high safety car rate typical of barrier-lined layouts.

documents.title: Marina Bay Singapore
documents.text:
Marina Bay Street Circuit (Singapore) — Circuit Notes, Pre- and Post-2023

Marina Bay is a genuine outlier in the reference table: it has the highest safety_car_frequency (≈0.9) and pit_lane_loss_time (≈24s) of any circuit on the calendar, and one of the highest DNF rates (≈0.2), reflecting a tight, humid, floodlit street circuit run at night with walls close to the racing line for almost the entire lap. Overtaking difficulty is rated high (≈0.8) in both configuration eras — this remains a circuit where track position, once established, is very hard to lose to a straightforward on-track pass.

The circuit is one of only two in the reference table (alongside Silverstone/Spa-type era changes generally) with a genuine layout change tracked as separate configuration eras: the pre-2023 layout included the Turn 16-19 chicane section around the old Singapore Sling area, which was removed for the 2023 race onward, simplifying that part of the lap and dropping the braking-zone count from 11 to 10 per lap. This is the calendar's clearest example of why the circuit reference table is keyed by configuration era rather than circuit name alone — treating pre- and post-2023 Marina Bay as identical would ignore a real, physical change to the track that a driver and car have to adapt to.

Given the combination of extreme heat/humidity, a bumpy street surface, and a high safety-car rate, races here are among the least "position stays static" of any hard-to-overtake circuit — not because passing is easy, but because incidents and cautions reshuffle the order more than at almost any other track.

documents.title: Melbourne
documents.text:
Albert Park Circuit (Melbourne) — Circuit Notes

Albert Park is run on public roads around a park lake, which is why it's flagged as a street-type circuit in the reference table (is_street_circuit = 1), even though it's wider and more flowing than a tight downtown street track like Monaco or Baku. Since the circuit's significant 2022 reprofiling (walls pushed back, several corners widened and reshaped specifically to encourage racing), overtaking difficulty here sits at a genuinely moderate level (≈0.5) rather than the much harder rating the old, tighter layout would have earned — this is a good example of a circuit where a real physical change should shift how much weight grid position carries relative to older seasons at the same track.

Safety car frequency is moderate (≈0.5) — the lakeside walls are unforgiving if a car gets it wrong, but the reprofiled corners give more margin than before. DNF rate is a fairly typical ≈0.12. Tyre degradation is on the low side (≈2/5), consistent with a track that rewards a smooth, flowing driving style over one that punishes the tyres through sustained high-lateral-load corners.

As an early-season race (often the second or third round), Melbourne shares Bahrain's characteristic of reflecting pre-season and prior-year form more than mid-season in-year development trends.

documents.title: Mexico City
documents.text:
Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez (Mexico City) — Circuit Notes

Mexico City's defining physical characteristic isn't captured directly in the standard reference-table columns but shapes everything about how the circuit behaves: it sits at roughly 2,200m altitude, among the highest of any F1 venue, where thinner air reduces both aerodynamic downforce and engine power, and teams run cars with unusually high wing levels to compensate. This is part of why overtaking difficulty is moderate (≈0.45) despite a long back straight into the stadium section's hard-braking Turn 1 — cars carry more drag than usual, which both aids slipstreaming on the straight and costs pure top speed.

The circuit has one of the shorter pit-lane loss times outside Montréal (≈18s), and DNF rate and safety car frequency are both fairly average (≈0.1 and ≈0.4). Tyre degradation is on the lower side (≈2/5) — the reduced grip and load from thin air actually means less absolute stress on the tyres than the corner speeds alone would suggest at sea level.

The final stadium section, run through a packed grandstand inside the old baseball stadium, is one of the most atmospheric and overtaking-relevant parts of the lap — cars are close together and slow enough there for genuine wheel-to-wheel racing even without a formal DRS zone.

documents.title: Miami
documents.text:
Miami International Autodrome — Circuit Notes

Miami is a purpose-built temporary circuit around the Hard Rock Stadium campus — classified as a street circuit (is_street_circuit = 1) even though, like Melbourne, it's wider and more permanent-feeling than a genuine downtown street track. Overtaking difficulty is moderate (≈0.5): there's a long back straight into a hard-braking zone that creates a real passing opportunity, offset by several tighter, wall-lined sections earlier in the lap where a mistake is costly.

Safety car frequency is on the higher side (≈0.6), consistent with most temporary/street-adjacent circuits — walls close to the racing line mean incidents are more likely to require a full safety car rather than resolving themselves. DNF rate (≈0.12) and tyre degradation (≈3/5) are both fairly typical mid-pack values. Rain is a minor factor (≈0.05) given the race's typical early-May date and South Florida climate, though it is not negligible the way it is at the Gulf-region rounds.

As with Jeddah, being a newer temporary layout means track evolution across the weekend (rubber laid down, grip building session to session) is more pronounced than at a permanent circuit with a stable, long-established surface.

documents.title: Monaco
documents.text:
Circuit de Monaco — Circuit Notes

Monaco is the single hardest circuit on the calendar to overtake at (overtaking_difficulty ≈ 0.95, the highest value in the reference table by a clear margin) — the track is barely wider than the cars in several places, run through the streets of the Principality with barriers immediately off the racing line and essentially no realistic passing zone under green-flag racing. This is the canonical example of a circuit where grid position is close to destiny: a driver who qualifies well is very likely to finish close to where they started, and a driver who qualifies poorly has almost no way to recover through overtaking alone (track position gained via pit-stop strategy or a safety car becomes disproportionately valuable instead).

Because passing is so difficult, the track's tyre degradation is rated the lowest in the calendar (≈1/5) — cars aren't fighting for position lap after lap the way they do at an overtaking-friendly circuit, so tyre life is rarely the limiting factor in a Monaco strategy the way pure track position is. The circuit is also the shortest on the calendar (3.337 km), meaning more laps are needed to cover full race distance, which raises the cumulative chance that a red flag, safety car, or VSC period (safety_car_frequency ≈ 0.6) reshuffles the strategic picture at some point in the race.

Monaco is the single clearest real-world illustration of why a model needs a grid-position-times-overtaking-difficulty interaction feature: the same grid position is worth far more here than at an easy-overtaking track like Monza.

documents.title: Montreal
documents.text:
Circuit Gilles Villeneuve (Montréal) — Circuit Notes

Montréal is a semi-permanent circuit on Île Notre-Dame, built around a mix of long straights and tight chicanes, with a famous wall at the final corner exit (the "Wall of Champions") that has ended more than one championship contender's race. It carries the shortest pit-lane loss time in the entire reference table (≈15.5s) — the pit lane here is unusually short relative to lap distance — which meaningfully changes the math on whether an extra pit stop is worth attempting compared to almost any other circuit on the calendar.

Overtaking difficulty is moderate (≈0.35), helped by long straights into hard-braking chicanes, but the circuit has the highest DNF rate in the reference table (≈0.2) and a high safety car frequency (≈0.8, second only to Marina Bay) — the combination of high speed, concrete walls very close to the racing line, and frequently changeable weather (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.2, one of the higher values outside of Spa/Silverstone/São Paulo) makes this one of the most unpredictable, caution-heavy rounds of the season.

Given the low pit-loss cost and high safety-car frequency, race-winning strategy at Montréal is disproportionately about being ready to react to a caution period rather than executing a pre-planned stint plan — a driver's realistic finishing position here is less "locked in" by qualifying than the raw overtaking-difficulty number alone would suggest.

documents.title: Monza
documents.text:
Autodromo Nazionale Monza — Circuit Notes

Monza is F1's classic "Temple of Speed" and has the lowest overtaking_difficulty rating in the entire reference table (≈0.2) — the layout is dominated by long straights (the front straight and the run through the Parabolica) into heavy-braking chicanes, which is about as favourable a geometry for passing as exists anywhere on the calendar. It also has the highest pit_lane_loss_time in the reference table (≈23s) — because lap times here are so short relative to other circuits, even a small pit-lane time loss represents a larger fraction of a lap than at a longer, slower circuit, which affects the undercut/overcut math.

Safety car frequency (≈0.2) and DNF rate (≈0.1) are both on the low side — Monza's chicanes are slow and forgiving by design, and its long straights don't carry the same wall-proximity risk as a street circuit at similar speed. Tyre degradation is comparatively low (≈2/5), since much of the lap is flat-out running rather than sustained cornering load.

Monza is the natural opposite pole to Monaco/Hungaroring/Zandvoort in any circuit-interaction analysis: grid position should matter comparatively little here, and a model that shows `grid_x_overtaking_difficulty` mattering far less at Monza than at those tracks is behaving exactly as the underlying racing reality suggests it should.

documents.title: Sao Paulo Interlagos
documents.text:
Autódromo José Carlos Pace (Interlagos, São Paulo) — Circuit Notes

Interlagos is a short, anti-clockwise permanent circuit (one of the few anti-clockwise tracks on the calendar, which creates unusual neck-load demands compared to most other rounds) with significant elevation change across the lap. Overtaking difficulty is on the easier side (≈0.3) — the start/finish straight into Turn 1 (the Senna S) is one of the most reliable overtaking spots in Formula 1, helped by the long uphill approach that makes slipstreaming effective.

Rain is a major factor here (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.35, tied with Spa for one of the highest in the reference table) — São Paulo's local climate produces sudden, intense tropical storms, and mixed or fully wet Interlagos races (including several famous title-deciding ones) are a recurring feature of the calendar rather than an exception. Safety car frequency (≈0.4) and DNF rate (≈0.12) are both moderately elevated, consistent with a short, technical lap where a rain-affected session compounds the normal risk of the technical Senna S and Turn 1 braking zone.

Given the combination of easy overtaking and frequent rain, Interlagos is one of the calendar's least "grid position is destiny" circuits — both the layout and the weather independently push toward more mixed-up, less predictable finishing orders than the average round.

documents.title: Sepang Kuala Lumpur
documents.text:
Sepang International Circuit, near Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Track length 5.543 km, 15 corners, 56 race laps. Formula 1 raced here as the Malaysian Grand Prix from 1999 to 2017; in 2026 it returns to host the Bahrain Grand Prix. None of this project's 2022-2026 data comes from Sepang, so every circuit value for it is an estimate from the layout and its earlier history, and should be revisited once a race has run.

Overtaking is relatively easy (difficulty ≈0.35): two long straights, the start-finish straight and the back straight, each end in heavy braking into a slow corner (Turn 1 and the Turn 15 hairpin), and the back straight into Turn 15 is the classic passing place. Cars can follow through the fast sweepers of the first sector less well.

Tyre degradation is high (≈4 on the 1-5 scale): an abrasive surface, long high-speed corners and track temperatures often above 50°C wear tyres quickly, which historically made two-stop races common.

Weather is the big unknown. Afternoon tropical thunderstorms are frequent (rain chance ≈0.35 in the reference table), heat and humidity make it one of the most physically demanding races for drivers, and the heat stresses brakes and power units, which is why its retirement rate is estimated above average (≈0.15). Safety cars have been moderately common (≈0.4), often weather-related.

documents.title: Shanghai
documents.text:
Shanghai International Circuit — Circuit Notes

Shanghai is a large, purpose-built permanent circuit distinguished by an unusually long, decreasing-radius Turn 1-2-3 complex (often compared to a snail shell) and one of the longest back straights on the calendar (≈1,170m) into a hard-braking hairpin. That combination keeps overtaking_difficulty at a moderate level (≈0.4) — the back straight is a genuine, reliable passing zone, similar in character to Austin or Bahrain.

Pit-lane loss time is on the higher side (≈22s), and tyre degradation is moderate (≈3/5) — the long, high-speed corners of the opening complex put real sustained load through the tyres despite the circuit's otherwise fairly conventional layout. Rain is a real if secondary factor (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.15), consistent with Shanghai's typically damp spring race date. Safety car frequency (≈0.4) and DNF rate (≈0.1) are both close to the calendar median.

Shanghai's return to the calendar after a multi-year absence (following construction and pandemic-era cancellations) means its more recent rows carry less accumulated recent track-form history for some drivers than a circuit that's been raced every year without interruption — worth remembering when a driver's `driver_track_form` value at this circuit looks unusually sparse.

documents.title: Silverstone
documents.text:
Silverstone Circuit — Circuit Notes

Silverstone is one of the fastest permanent circuits on the calendar, built on a former WWII airfield, with a sequence of high-speed corners (Maggotts, Becketts, Chapel) that are among the most demanding in Formula 1. Despite that speed, overtaking difficulty is on the lower side (≈0.35) — the long Hangar Straight into the Stowe/Vale braking zone, plus the Wellington Straight, both create real passing opportunities that offset the technical middle sector.

Tyre degradation is rated at the top of the scale (≈4/5, tied with Bahrain/Barcelona/Spa/Suzuka) — the sustained high-speed lateral loading through Maggotts-Becketts-Chapel is some of the hardest cornering load tyres see anywhere on the calendar. Silverstone also has the highest rain_race_frequency among the "permanent circuit" group (≈0.25) — British summer weather is famously unpredictable, and a wet or mixed-conditions Silverstone race is a regular occurrence rather than a rare event, which is part of why practice and qualifying pace here can be a noisier predictor of race-day pace than at a more climatically stable venue.

Safety car frequency (≈0.3) and DNF rate (≈0.1) are both moderate — the circuit has generous, modern run-off in most places, but the sheer cornering speed means the corners that do punish a mistake tend to do so decisively.

documents.title: Spa
documents.text:
Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps — Circuit Notes

Spa is the longest circuit on the F1 calendar (7.004 km) and, alongside Bahrain, has the lowest overtaking_difficulty rating in the reference table (≈0.25) — the run from Eau Rouge/Raidillon up the Kemmel Straight into the Les Combes braking zone is one of the most famous and reliable overtaking opportunities in motorsport, and the long lap also means multiple further passing zones elsewhere. This is a track where a poor qualifying result is one of the most recoverable in the whole calendar.

Spa has the highest rain_race_frequency of any circuit in the reference table (≈0.35) — the Ardennes forest region is famous for its own microclimate, where it can be raining at one part of the circuit and dry at another within the same lap, which is a genuinely unique strategic challenge (mixed-conditions tyre choice) that few other circuits present at this scale. Tyre degradation is rated high (≈3/5, and effectively higher in practice given the very high average speed and long straights that load tyres differently than a technical circuit). Safety car frequency (≈0.5) and DNF rate (≈0.12) are both elevated by the combination of high average speed and a track that, despite modern run-off at Eau Rouge, still punishes a mistake at the wrong moment severely.

Spa is a strong counter-example to Monaco/Hungaroring/Zandvoort in any circuit-interaction SHAP analysis — grid position should matter comparatively little here relative to those tracks, precisely because overtaking is genuinely easy.

documents.title: Spielberg
documents.text:
Red Bull Ring (Spielberg) — Circuit Notes

The Red Bull Ring is one of the shortest permanent lap distances on the calendar (4.318 km) set in the Styrian hills, with dramatic elevation change and just three real braking zones per lap (the lowest braking-zone count in the reference table) — most of the circuit is flowing, high-speed corners connected by short straights. That layout keeps overtaking difficulty moderate (≈0.4): the three hard-braking zones are all genuine passing opportunities, but there's comparatively little of the lap where a pass can actually be attempted.

Tyre degradation is on the higher side (≈3/5) for a circuit this short, since the fast, sweeping corners put sustained load through the tyres despite the low overall lap distance. Safety car frequency (≈0.3) and DNF rate (≈0.1) are both fairly average, and rain is a moderate factor (≈0.1) given the circuit's mountainous setting, where weather can change quickly within a race weekend.

Because the lap is so short, drivers spend a larger fraction of total race distance in genuinely high-speed, low-margin-for-error corners than at a longer circuit — small qualifying-pace deficits tend to compound less dramatically over a race distance here than at a circuit with more low-speed technical sections to lose time in.

documents.title: Suzuka
documents.text:
Suzuka International Racing Course — Circuit Notes

Suzuka is one of the most technically demanding circuits on the calendar, famous for its figure-eight layout (the only crossover circuit in F1) and the high-speed Esses/130R sequence. Overtaking difficulty sits at a moderate level (≈0.5) — the hairpin and the final chicane both offer real passing chances, but the flowing middle sector is unforgiving of a car that isn't fundamentally quick, so grid position still carries meaningful weight even where a pass is technically possible.

Tyre degradation is rated at the top of the scale (≈4/5) — the sustained high-speed direction changes through the Esses put some of the highest lateral load on tyres anywhere on the calendar. Rain is a significant factor (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.3) given Suzuka's typical autumn date and Japan's typhoon-season weather patterns — wet-weather Suzuka races, including red-flagged sessions, are a recurring feature of the calendar rather than a rare event.

Safety car frequency (≈0.3) and DNF rate (≈0.1) are both moderate, reflecting a circuit that rewards precision and punishes a lack of it, without being as consistently incident-prone as a street circuit. Suzuka's combination of high degradation and moderate overtaking difficulty makes tyre strategy and pit-stop timing a particularly important explanatory factor here relative to pure grid position.

documents.title: Yas Island Abudhabi
documents.text:
Yas Marina Circuit (Yas Island, Abu Dhabi) — Circuit Notes

Yas Marina hosts the traditional season finale and underwent a significant 2021 reprofiling (several corners in the final sector were reshaped and widened specifically to improve overtaking, after the circuit had developed a reputation as one of the hardest to pass at on the calendar). Since that change, overtaking_difficulty is rated at a moderate level (≈0.55) — a meaningful improvement on the old layout's reputation, though still tighter than a genuine power circuit like Monza or Bahrain.

DNF rate is among the lowest in the reference table (≈0.08) — the circuit has generous, modern run-off throughout, and by the time of the season finale, most reliability issues that are going to surface across a season have typically already done so on cars that make it this far. Safety car frequency (≈0.3) and tyre degradation (≈2/5) are both moderate, and rain is a non-factor given the UAE desert climate (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.0).

Being the final round of the season means this circuit's rows often carry extra significance for championship-outcome context even though the reference table itself only captures track characteristics — a driver's recent form and season-long track-form features going into Abu Dhabi reflect a full season's accumulated data, more than at any earlier round.

documents.title: Zandvoort
documents.text:
Circuit Zandvoort — Circuit Notes

Zandvoort returned to the F1 calendar in 2021 after a long absence, reconfigured with banked corners (most notably the final corner) inspired by American oval racing, in an attempt to improve overtaking at what is fundamentally a narrow, dune-constrained old-school circuit. Despite the banking, overtaking_difficulty is rated the second-highest in the entire reference table (≈0.85, behind only Monaco) — the track is simply too narrow through most of its lap for the banking alone to fix the underlying passing problem, and the circuit has few genuine straight-into-hard-braking zones.

Tyre degradation is moderate (≈3/5), and rain is a real factor given the North Sea coastal location (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.15) — Dutch coastal weather can turn quickly, and the dunes that give the circuit its character also create localized wind effects that can catch drivers out. Safety car frequency is moderate (≈0.4), broadly in line with other narrow permanent circuits with limited run-off in key corners.

Given how close Zandvoort's overtaking difficulty sits to Monaco's, a well-tuned model should show grid position and grid-times-overtaking-difficulty interaction features carrying similarly outsized weight at both — Zandvoort is a useful check on whether a circuit-aware feature is really learning "hard to pass" rather than just memorizing "this is Monaco."

FIA Formula 1  
Driving Standards Guidelines 
26 February 2026 
v 01 
These are GUIDELINES and NOT REGULATIONS 
At all times the Stewards will adjudicate based upon the Regulations, but decisions will be informed and 
guided by these guidelines and the experience of their Driver Stewards. 
If it has been established from points A and B below, that an overtaking driver has priority, it is the 
responsibility of the defending driver to avoid a collision or forcing off the overtaking driver. 
However, many incidents require subjective judgement and therefore the following important caveats 
apply: 
1. A car being overtaken, or performing an overtake, cannot simply “disappear” . 
2. A lock up or small steering correction do not necessarily imply a driver has lost control 
3. An apparent temporary loss of control , or a lock up,  may be due to an attempt to avoid a 
collision, or simply the “laws of physics” . 
4. The apex may vary depending on the racing line taken and/or the nature of the corner itself. 
As a general policy, penalty points will be applied only for dangerous, reckless or apparently deliberate 
actions resulting in a collision, or other unacceptable driving behaviour or unsportsmanlike behaviour on 
the part of the driver 
Attention is also drawn to the important note in Point F on page 3, for defending drivers who leave the 
track whilst defending a position. 
A. Overtaking on the INSIDE of a corner  
To be entitled to be given room when overtaking on the INSIDE, the overtaking car must: 
i) Have its front axle AT LEAST ALONGSIDE THE MIRROR of the other car PRIOR TO AND AT THE 
APEX 
ii) Be driven in a fully controlled manner particularly from entry to apex and not have “dived in”. 
iii) In the Stewards’ estimation, have taken a reasonable racing line and been able to complete the 
move whilst remaining within track limits. 
B. Overtaking on the OUTSIDE of a corner 
Overtaking on the outside will always be viewed as a more difficult manoeuvre to accomplish.  
To be entitled to be given room, including at the exit, when overtaking on the OUTSIDE, the overtaking 
car must: 
i) Have its front axle AHEAD OF THE FRONT AXLE of the other car AT THE APEX. 
ii) Be driven in a controlled manner from entry, to apex, and to exit. 
iii) Be able to make the corner within track limits.

v 01 
Note(s): 
On long radius curves, provided point (ii) above is complied with, the Stewards will treat each case 
on its merits particularly where there is no defined apex or there are multiple apexes.  
C. Chicanes and S-Bends 
The above guides for INSIDE and OUTSIDE may apply for each element of the combination.  
Generally, priority will be given to the first corner element. However other factors such as the 
sequence of corners will be considered holistically by the Stewards when assessing the right to the 
corner. 
IMPORTANT NOTES FOR A, B & C ABOVE: 
Racing is a dynamic process. Although these guidelines indicate specific relative positions of the 
cars at various points, the Stewards will always look at how the situation played out in total when 
reviewing an incident. For example: 
i) How did the cars get to the incident? (E.g. late braking, diving in, moving under braking.) 
ii) Was the manoeuvre late or “optimistic”? 
iii) What could the drivers reasonably see, know, or anticipate? 
iv) Do we believe the manoeuvre could be completed on the track? 
v) Was there understeer / oversteer / locking?  
vi) Was there an attempt to avoid a collision? 
vii) Did either car release the brakes in order to attempt to gain priority. 
viii) Did someone position / handle their car in a way that contributed to the incident? 
ix) Did the type of corner contribute to the incident? (e.g. camber, kerbs, curve, apexes) 
x) What were the relative tyres / tyre age / grip? 
D. Track Limits 
It is considered that respecting track limits is important for both racing fairness and safety, thus 
Article B1.8.6 will be strictly enforced: 
“Drivers must make every reasonable effort to use the track at all times and may not leave the 
track without a justifiable reason. 
Drivers will be judged to have left the track if no part of the car remains in contact with it and, for 
the avoidance of doubt, the white lines defining the track edges are considered to be part of the 
track, but the kerbs are not... .” 
Note(s): 
In the case of an infringement in Sprint Qualifying or Qualifying, the lap time will be deleted, and the 
time of the subsequent lap if it is deemed that there could be a benefit.  
For the Sprint Session and Race, acknowledging that racing is a dynamic process, invalid lap times 
will be deleted and a “three strikes” system shall normally be applied prior to issuance of a Black & 
White Flag or penalty under Article B1.9.5. For the avoidance of doubt any invalid lap will be deleted 
and counted as a “strike” with the following EXCEPTIONS:

chunks.title: 2026 Driving Standards Guidelines
chunks.text:
26 February 2026 
v 01 
i) If a driver exceeds track limits following an obvious loss of control. 
ii) If a driver exceeds track limits in order to avoid a collision e.g. Typical Lap 1, Turn 1 incident. 
iii) If a driver has been considered to be “forced off” by another car (in a decision of the stewards) 
iv) If a driver exceeds track limits and is penalised for gaining a lasting advantage or unsafe re-join. 
v) If a driver exceeds track limits during an incident which is penalised for any other reason. E.g. if 
a driver  exceeds track limits during an incident for which they are penalised for causing a 
collision.  
vi)  In the context of an overtaking manoeuvre, be that failed or completed, i f a driver leaves the 
track but clearly gains no advantage, the Stewards retain the discretion to determine that no 
strike will be applied. 
It is noted that the imposition of a “strike” remains at the sole discretion of the Stewards and that on 
some occasions, where it is considered  a car has left the track without a justifiable reason for 
specific, intentional or unsportsmanlike reasons, a penalty rather than a strike may be imposed. 
E. Impeding 
Not only will Article B4.1.1 be enforced, but drivers are reminded of Article B1.8.5: 
“At no time may an F1 Car be driven unnecessarily slowly, erratically or in a manner which could 
be deemed potentially dangerous to other drivers or any other person.” 
F. Giving back a lasting advantage 
The Procedure in Article B1.8.6 will be strictly applied: 
“Should a car leave the track the driver may re -join, however, this may only be done when it is 
safe to do so and without gaining any lasting advantage. At the absolute discretion of the Race 
Director a driver may be given the opportunity to give back the whole of any advantage he gained 
by leaving the track. ” 
Note(s): 
If, while defending a position, a car leaves the track (or cuts a chicane) and re -joins in the same 
position, it will generally be considered by the stewards as having gained a lasting advantage and 
therefore, generally, the position should be conceded. It will be the sole discretion of the Stewards 
to determine if the driver of a car is “defending a position.” See also point D above. 
G. Moving on the Straight 
Appendix L, Chapter IV, Article 2b states: 
“More than one change of direction to defend a position is not permitted.  Any driver moving 
back towards the racing line, having earlier defended his position off-line, should leave at least 
one car width between his own car and the edge of the track on the approach to the corner. “

chunks.title: 2026 Driving Standards Guidelines
chunks.text:
“However, manoeuvres liable to hinder other drivers, such as deliberate crowding of a car 
beyond the edge of the track or any other abnormal change of direction, are strictly prohibited. 
Any driver who appears guilty of any of the above offences will be reported to the Stewards.”

Guidelines

©2026 Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile 
26 February 2026 
v 01 
Note(s): 
In this context, moves intended to break the slipstream of a following car when the following car is a 
safe distance behind, considering relative speeds and position on the track, may be acceptable.  
H. Moving under Braking 
When defending, there must be no change in direction by the defending car, after the deceleration 
phase has commenced, except to follow the racing line.  
I. Re-joining the Track 
Maintaining racing speeds in the run-off area is not acceptable. Cars on track must not be forced to 
change speed or line to avoid a re-joining car. 
J. Safety Car 
To avoid the likelihood of accidents before the Safety Car returns to the pits, Article B5.13.6 will be 
enforced as shown below: 
“In order to avoid the likelihood of accidents before the safety car returns to the pits, from the 
point at which the orange lights on the safety car are extinguished drivers must proceed at a pace 
which involves no erratic acceleration or braking nor any other manoeuvre which is likely to 
endanger other drivers or impede the restart”.

chunks.title: 2026 Driving Standards Guidelines
chunks.text:
Note(s): 
The actions of the lead driver in particular can have a significant impact on the safety of the restart 
procedure. Although the leading driver has both the right to dictate pace as well as to choose the 
point at which to accelerate, this does not relieve them  of their responsibility to avoid creating a 
potentially dangerous situation as defined in the Code Appendix L Ch IV 2(e).  
K. Blue Flags 
Appendix L, Chapter IV, Article 2a states: 
“A car alone on the track may use the full width of the said track, however, as soon as it is caught 
by a car which is about to lap it the driver must allow the faster driver past at the first possible 
opportunity. 
If the driver who has been caught does not seem to make full use of the rear -view mirrors, flag 
marshals will display the waved blue flag to indicate that the faster driver wants to overtake. Any 
driver who appears to ignore the blue flags will be reported to the Stewards “ 
Note(s): 
Upon receiving a blue flag, the driver must allow the car behind to overtake at the earliest possible 
opportunity.  Some tolerance will be allowed, in order to allow  the overtake to occur on the next 
straight section of track.   
Driving Standards 
Guidelines 
 Page 5

©2026 Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile

chunks.title: 2026 Driving Standards Guidelines
chunks.text:
26 February 2026 
v 01 
Failure to allow the overtake on the next straight section of track will likely be considered a breach. 
The following situations will almost certainly be considered a breach: 
i) If the overtake occurs after the car has passed 8 consecutive light panels 
ii) If an overtake is delayed by  the car being lapped  in order to receive OVERTAKE from the car 
lapping. 
L. Yellow & Double Yellow Flags 
It is considered that respect of Yellow and Double Yellow flags is critical for safety and important for 
racing fairness, thus Article B1.8.4a & b will be strictly enforced: 
“a. Single Waved Yellow Flag: Any driver passing through a waved yellow flag marshalling sector 
must reduce their speed and be prepared to change direction. In order for the stewards to 
be satisfied that any such driver has complied with these requirements the y are expected 
to have braked earlier and/or discernibly reduced speed in the relevant marshalling sector. 
b. Double Waved Yellow Flag: Any driver passing through a double waved yellow flag 
marshalling sector must reduce speed significantly and be prepared to change direction or 
stop. In order for the stewards to be satisfied that any such driver has complied with these 
requirements it must be clear that the driver has not attempted to set a meaningful lap time 
on the relevant lap...” 
Note(s): 
i) The onus rests with the driver to demonstrate a sufficient reduction of speed to satisfy the rules. 
ii) The extent of speed reduction considered acceptable may vary depending on the conditions 
and visibility of and through the incident. 
iii) The requirement that a driver be prepared to stop in the case of Double Waved Yellow Flags 
means that the speed reduction must be significantly and noticeably greater than in the case of 
a Single Waved Yellow Flag. 
iv) In evaluating compliance with the rules, the Stewards will pay close attention to the extent of 
driver input (throttle pedal, brake pedal, steering angle) prior to and through the incident 
location. 
v) It will be up to the driver to demonstrate to the Stewards, via the “driver input” referred to above 
or by the method below, that they have complied with the regulations. 
vi) One method of demonstrating compliance (but not the only method) would be, in the case of a 
Single Waved Yellow Flag, an increase in the time taken to traverse the flag sector, of at least 5% 
compared to the driver’s previous lap(s) under similar conditions.   
vii) Similarly, one method of demonstrating a significant reduction of speed and preparedness to 
stop, (again, not the only method) would be, in the case of Double Waved Yellow Flags, an 
increase in the time taken to traverse the flag sector, of at least 15% compared to the driver’s 
previous lap(s) under similar conditions.  
viii) In considering what is a lap under ‘similar conditions’ the Stewards will take into account tyre 
compound, tyre condition, fuel load, energy deployment and weather conditions. 
ix) Any car losing control under a yellow flag or double yellow flag will usually be investigated.

26 February 2026 
v 01 
APPENDIX 1: CONTEXT OF THESE GUIDELINES 
In 2022, responding to requests from the Formula 1 drivers for clarity on how the F1 Stewards would 
interpret the rules in certain circumstances, it was agreed that a set of Driving Standards would be 
established which would act as GUIDELINES for investiga tion of incidents and application of any 
penalties.   
The FIA Drivers Commission commenced work to integrate the existing Formula 1 Driving Standards 
Guidelines into a comprehensive document that could apply to all circuit racing categories. 
Of key importance to the FIA Drivers Commission is the desire to ensure that the younger drivers in lower 
categories are subjected to the same standards as will apply when they eventually graduate to the highest 
levels of the sport.  
The core objectives of the FIA Drivers Commission, in the publication across all championships, of 
driving standards guidelines is to facilitate and promote: 
• Safe racing  
• Hard and competitive racing  
• Fair racing  
• Sporting justice  
• Consistency across all categories  
• Standardization of driving standards and race direction operation across all 
categories.  
Rationale 
i) Overtaking should be incentivized and defending a position unfairly or dangerously is not 
acceptable.  
ii) It is very important that junior drivers race with the same guidelines as F1. However, less 
tolerance should be applied because the risk of an accident is higher due to their lesser  
experience. Being stricter in applying the rules in lower formulas is essential for junior driver 
development.  
iii) It is imperative to reiterate that the guidelines will be applied during the entirety of the event. 
The Race Director and Stewards will be available to clarify any questions that drivers and teams 
may have with regards to the guidelines.  
iv) The Stewards and Driver Advisor will, if possible, always attend the drivers briefing.  
v) Application of the guidelines should be enforced throughout the event, with particular attention 
to respect of yellow flags and track limits.  
vi) Regarding track limits, the Stewards will always satisfy themselves that the infractions are 
clear. Drivers will be given the benefit of the doubt when the infraction is not clear.  
vii) A Driver Steward or Driver Advisor should be appointed for each category or series [This is the 
case for Formula 1].

Note 1  Penalties for a first offence in a two- year period, except in cases of misconduct  towards officials (Article 12.2.1.l) or breach of ISC Article 12.2.1.n, may be reduced due to 
mitigations, which may include imposing a fully suspended penalty or, in exceptional circumstances, issuing a formal warning. 
Note 2  Controlled Environments include, but are not limited to, media interviews, press conferences, and podiums ceremonies. Non-Controlled Environments include, but are not 
limited to, radio transmissions between car and team, recordings made while on circuit. Alleged breaches of ISC Articles 12.2.1.f or 12.2.1.l that occur in “non -controlled” 
environments may be treated as private conversations, except where multiple breaches occur within a short period of time, involve racial or discriminatory language, or 
include abuse of officials. 
Note 3  The fine of €5,000 may be reduced or increased based on the mitigating or aggravating circumstances described in Appendix B of the ISC, specifically Notes 4 and 5. Copied 
below for reference: 
4.  Mitigating circumstances can include, but are not limited to:  
a.  The status of the driver (e.g., unpaid amateur, rookie professional, or high-
profile, long-standing professional driver);  
b.  The status or profile of the championship in which the offence occurred;  
c.  Personal circumstances relating to the alleged offender such as:  
i.  reaction to offensive, aggressive or abusive behaviour by another,  
ii.  in the case of ISC Art 12.2.1.p, a pre- advised medical condition 
verified by medical practitioner.  
d.  The alleged offender’s previous record of good behaviour.  
5.  Aggravating circumstance can include, but are not limited to:  
a.  Premeditated actions as determined by the Stewards. 
b.  Multiple offenses, especially if occurring within a short period of 
time. 
The fine of €5,000 may be increased based multiples of 2 or 3 when the seriousness of the offence warrants a higher penalty.
