chunks.title: Austin
chunks.text:
Circuit of the Americas (Austin) — Circuit Notes
COTA was purpose-built for F1 with a mix of corner styles deliberately inspired by other famous circuits (its Turn 1 uphill esses draw comparisons to Silverstone's Maggotts-Becketts, and its infield section nods to several classic European tracks). Overtaking difficulty is moderate (≈0.35) — the long back straight into Turn 12 is a reliable passing zone, similar in concept to Austin's fellow modern-build permanent circuits like Shanghai and Bahrain.
Tyre degradation is moderate (≈3/5), safety car frequency and DNF rate are both fairly average for the calendar (≈0.3 and ≈0.1), and rain is a real if secondary factor (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.15) given the circuit's Texas autumn date, which can bring sudden storms. Pit-lane loss time (≈21s) sits near the calendar median, making strategy calculations here comparatively "textbook" relative to outlier circuits like Montréal (very short pit loss) or Monza (very long pit loss).
COTA is a useful calendar "baseline" circuit in modeling terms — none of its reference-table values are extreme outliers in either direction, so it's a reasonable circuit to compare a more unusual track's characteristics against when explaining why a prediction differs from the calendar median.

chunks.title: Bahrain Sakhir
chunks.text:
Bahrain International Circuit (Sakhir) — Circuit Notes
Bahrain International Circuit is a permanent desert facility, not a street circuit, and it sits at the easy end of the overtaking-difficulty spectrum (overtaking_difficulty ≈ 0.25, tied for the lowest in the calendar alongside Spa). Its long straights (up to ~1,100m) feed into wide, heavy-braking corners with multiple lines through the apex, which is exactly the geometry that makes passing straightforward relative to a street track. This is a big part of why grid position tends to matter less here than at a track like Monaco — a driver who qualifies poorly still has real chances to recover position during the race.
The abrasive desert surface and sustained high-speed cornering load make this one of the higher tyre-degradation circuits on the calendar (tyre_degradation_level ≈ 4/5), so strategy and stint management carry real weight in the finishing order, not just one-lap pace. Safety car interventions are moderate (≈0.3 frequency) — the run-off areas are generous by modern standards, which keeps incident-triggered cautions from being as constant as on a street track, but the fast corners and high tyre wear still produce enough incidents to matter. Rain is essentially a non-factor here (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.0) given the desert climate, so weather-driven strategy swings that show up at wetter European rounds don't apply at Bahrain.

chunks.title: Bahrain Sakhir
chunks.text: Because the season often opens here, Bahrain also tends to be a track where pre-season form is least tested by in-season development — form features reflect the prior year's competitive order more directly than at later rounds.

chunks.title: Baku
chunks.text:
Baku City Circuit — Circuit Notes
Baku combines a tight, twisting old-city section with the longest straight on the calendar (≈2,200m) running alongside the Caspian Sea — one of the most unusual layout combinations in Formula 1. That long straight, feeding into a hard-braking zone, is a genuine overtaking opportunity, which keeps overtaking_difficulty at a moderate level (≈0.35) despite how unforgiving the narrow old-town section is if a driver gets it wrong.
Baku has the highest safety_car_frequency in the entire reference table (≈0.7) and one of the highest DNF rates (≈0.18) — the combination of very high top speed on the straight and wall-lined, low-run-off corners in the castle section means incidents here are frequent and tend to require full safety car neutralization rather than resolving under local yellow flags. The circuit's braking-zone count is low (only 4) relative to its length, which is part of why it doesn't behave like a typical technical street track — most of the lap is either flat-out or a single hard braking event, rather than the constant direction changes of a track like Singapore.
Tyre degradation is on the lower side (≈2/5), since the layout doesn't put sustained lateral load through the tyres the way a flowing permanent circuit does — most of the stress here is longitudinal, from the very hard braking zones rather than cornering load.

chunks.title: Barcelona
chunks.text:
Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya — Circuit Notes
Barcelona was, for decades, F1's primary pre-season testing venue, so teams historically know this track's characteristics better than almost anywhere else on the calendar — a fact that shows up in how predictable the competitive order tends to be here relative to a novel street circuit. It's a permanent circuit with a demanding mix of high-speed and medium-speed corners, and it's rated among the higher end of the tyre-degradation scale (≈4/5) — the long, high-load corners (particularly the final sector's sustained cornering) put significant lateral stress through the tyres over a race distance.
Overtaking difficulty is moderate-to-high (≈0.65) — there is a DRS zone into Turn 1, but the technical middle sector offers few genuine passing chances, so track position gained in the first few corners tends to hold. Safety car frequency is the lowest in the entire reference table (≈0.2), and DNF rate is similarly low (≈0.1) — this is a circuit with generous run-off and a layout that punishes pace more than it punishes small mistakes, so races here tend to run green from start to finish more often than almost anywhere else on the calendar.
Because degradation is high but overtaking is hard, strategy (undercut/overcut timing) tends to matter more here than outright overtaking on-track — a well-timed pit stop can gain track position in a way that a wheel-to-wheel move often can't.

chunks.title: Budapest
chunks.text:
Hungaroring (Budapest) — Circuit Notes
The Hungaroring is a tight, twisty permanent circuit often described as "Monaco without the walls" — there's more run-off than a street circuit, but the layout offers almost no long straights and a constant sequence of medium-speed corners that make following (let alone passing) another car extremely difficult. Overtaking difficulty is rated near the top of the calendar (≈0.8, just behind Zandvoort and well behind only Monaco) — this is one of the clearest examples of a permanent circuit behaving like a street track in terms of how much grid position dictates the finishing order.
Because the layout is so technical and low-speed relative to the rest of the calendar, DNF rate is among the lowest in the reference table (≈0.08) — there simply aren't many high-consequence corners to crash out of, races here tend to be processional and low-drama by F1 standards. Tyre degradation is moderate (≈3/5), and rain is a real if not dominant factor (≈0.1) given the mid-summer Central European date.
Because overtaking is so hard here, qualifying performance is an especially strong predictor of finishing position — a driver who has a bad Saturday at the Hungaroring has fewer realistic paths back through the field than almost anywhere else on the calendar besides Monaco.

chunks.title: Imola
chunks.text:
Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari (Imola) — Circuit Notes
Imola is a fast, old-school permanent circuit with very few genuine overtaking zones — most of the lap is flowing, high-commitment corners taken in quick succession, with only a couple of real braking-zone passing opportunities (notably into Tamburello and the Variante Alta chicane). That's why overtaking_difficulty is rated high here (≈0.75), closer to Hungaroring and Zandvoort than to a power circuit like Monza. Grid position and clean qualifying pace matter disproportionately at tracks like this, because a driver who gets stuck behind a slower car often has nowhere to pass until the car ahead makes a mistake.
Tyre degradation is moderate-to-high (≈3/5) given the sustained high-speed direction changes, and rain shows up here more than at the desert/Gulf rounds (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.15) — Imola sits in a part of Europe with genuinely unpredictable spring weather, and a wet or drying track at this circuit tends to scramble the grid more than usual precisely because overtaking is already hard in the dry, so drivers who gain track position in mixed conditions are much harder to repass once it dries.
Safety car frequency (≈0.5) and DNF rate (≈0.15) are both on the higher side for a permanent (non-street) circuit — the lack of run-off in several places (this remains one of the more old-fashioned tracks on the calendar) means an off-track excursion is more likely to end a car's race than at a modern Tilke-designed layout.

chunks.title: Jeddah
chunks.text:
Jeddah Corniche Circuit — Circuit Notes
Jeddah is one of the fastest street circuits ever built for Formula 1 — narrow, wall-lined, and taken at very high average speed despite being a temporary/semi-permanent street layout (is_street_circuit = 1). That combination is precisely why it carries one of the highest safety-car frequencies in the calendar (safety_car_frequency ≈ 0.6): walls punish even small errors, and at the speeds this track is run, an off-line moment easily becomes a barrier contact rather than a spun car that rejoins under its own power. DNF rate is correspondingly elevated (≈0.15).
Overtaking difficulty sits in the middle of the calendar (≈0.55) — there are genuine passing zones into the long back-straight braking area, but the blind, high-speed corners elsewhere on the lap punish a driver who commits to a move without a clear picture of what's ahead, so overtakes are riskier to attempt than the number alone suggests. Tyre degradation is comparatively low (≈2/5) for a track run at such high average speed, since the layout favours flowing, low-slip-angle corners over the sustained lateral loading that chews through tyres elsewhere.
Because Jeddah is a street track, track evolution across the weekend is significant — the surface rubbers in a lot between first practice and qualifying, which is part of why practice pace here is a noisier predictor of race pace than at a permanent circuit with a more stable surface.

chunks.title: Las Vegas
chunks.text:
Las Vegas Strip Circuit — Circuit Notes
Las Vegas joined the calendar in 2023 as a purpose-built street circuit run at night down the middle of the Strip, past the Bellagio fountains and the Sphere. It has the second-longest straight in the reference table (≈1,900m, behind only Baku), which creates a genuine, high-speed overtaking opportunity, keeping overtaking_difficulty at a moderate level (≈0.35) despite being a street circuit — most street tracks (Monaco, Singapore, Jeddah) skew harder to pass at than this.
The circuit is run very late at night in cold desert-adjacent conditions (Vegas in November), which is atypical for F1 — track temperatures are unusually low for the sport, and tyre_degradation_level is rated on the lower side (≈2/5) partly as a result, since cold track temperatures reduce the aggressive degradation seen at hotter rounds. Safety car frequency is moderate (≈0.4), and rain is effectively a non-factor given the desert climate (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.0).
As one of the newest circuits in the reference table, Las Vegas has comparatively little accumulated historical race data behind it relative to a long-established venue — its row is a real, current-generation street circuit rather than a rough inaugural-year estimate, but the model still has fewer prior seasons to draw driver/team track-form history from here than at, say, Monza or Silverstone.

chunks.title: Le Castellet
chunks.text:
Circuit Paul Ricard (Le Castellet) — Circuit Notes
Paul Ricard hosted the French Grand Prix through 2022 before dropping off the calendar — it's included in the reference table with a valid range ending in 2022, so it's a good example of the table's era-keying handling a circuit's departure rather than treating it as a permanent fixture. It's a wide, modern permanent circuit with the distinctive asphalt run-off "safety zones" instead of gravel traps, and one of the longer straights outside Baku/Las Vegas (≈1,800m) feeding the Mistral straight braking zone.
Overtaking difficulty was moderate-to-high (≈0.6) — the wide track surface actually made side-by-side racing easier in some sections than the number alone suggests, but a genuinely quick middle sector limited how often drivers found themselves close enough to attempt a pass. The circuit had the lowest DNF rate (≈0.08) and one of the lowest safety-car frequencies (≈0.1) in the whole reference table — the asphalt run-off areas meant an off-track excursion very rarely ended a car's race or triggered a caution, since a driver could simply rejoin without contact.
Because it's no longer on the calendar, this circuit's data only ever appears as historical training rows (2022 and earlier) — the model will never need to produce a live prediction here, but the historical rows remain useful, leakage-safe training signal for the general relationship between circuit layout and outcome.

chunks.title: Lusail Qatar
chunks.text:
Lusail International Circuit (Qatar) — Circuit Notes
Lusail is a fast, flowing desert circuit originally built for motorcycle racing before being adapted for F1, with a long sequence of high-speed corners that place unusually high demand on tyres — tyre_degradation_level is rated at the top of the scale (≈4/5), among the highest in the reference table alongside Bahrain, Barcelona, Silverstone, and Suzuka. Overtaking difficulty is moderate (≈0.55) — there are passing opportunities, but the high-speed nature of most corners means a driver needs a real pace advantage, not just a slipstream, to make a move stick.
Safety car and DNF rates are both fairly typical for the calendar (≈0.3 and ≈0.1 respectively), and rain is effectively a non-factor given the Gulf desert climate (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.0), similar to Bahrain and Jeddah. As a floodlit night race on a circuit built for two-wheeled racing, track temperature management (rather than rain) is the more significant weather-adjacent variable here — track temp tends to be more stable and cooler at night than an equivalent daytime desert race, which affects tyre degradation modeling more than any rain-probability feature would.
Given the combination of high degradation and moderate overtaking difficulty, race outcomes here tend to be shaped as much by who manages their tyres best across a long stint as by grid position alone.

chunks.title: Madrid
chunks.text:
Madrid Street Circuit (IFEMA / MADRING) — Circuit Notes
Madrid joined the F1 calendar in 2026 as a new street circuit built around the IFEMA convention center complex, combining permanent-facility sections with temporary street segments — a hybrid layout style similar in spirit to Miami and Las Vegas rather than a pure downtown street track like Monaco or Baku. Its reference-table row is explicitly flagged as an inaugural-circuit estimate: with zero prior seasons of real race data at the time it was added, its proxy values (overtaking_difficulty ≈ 0.6, safety_car_frequency ≈ 0.5, pit_lane_loss_time ≈ 21s, tyre_degradation_level ≈ 3/5) are reasoned from public layout facts and comparison to similar hybrid circuits, not derived from historical results the way an established circuit's row is.
As is standard for the reference table, this row should be revisited and refined once real race data accumulates — a circuit's actual overtaking and safety-car behavior often differs from pre-race estimates in ways that only show up once cars have genuinely raced there under representative conditions (tyre wear patterns, real overtaking attempts, real incident history). Until then, any prediction or explanation involving Madrid should be understood as resting on a rougher circuit-characteristics foundation than a prediction for a well-established venue like Silverstone or Monza.

chunks.title: Madrid
chunks.text: Being a street circuit (is_street_circuit = 1) with an urban setting, Madrid also inherits the general street-circuit pattern seen elsewhere in this dataset: comparatively pronounced track evolution across a race weekend as the surface rubbers in, and a moderate-to-high safety car rate typical of barrier-lined layouts.

chunks.title: Marina Bay Singapore
chunks.text:
Marina Bay Street Circuit (Singapore) — Circuit Notes, Pre- and Post-2023
Marina Bay is a genuine outlier in the reference table: it has the highest safety_car_frequency (≈0.9) and pit_lane_loss_time (≈24s) of any circuit on the calendar, and one of the highest DNF rates (≈0.2), reflecting a tight, humid, floodlit street circuit run at night with walls close to the racing line for almost the entire lap. Overtaking difficulty is rated high (≈0.8) in both configuration eras — this remains a circuit where track position, once established, is very hard to lose to a straightforward on-track pass.
The circuit is one of only two in the reference table (alongside Silverstone/Spa-type era changes generally) with a genuine layout change tracked as separate configuration eras: the pre-2023 layout included the Turn 16-19 chicane section around the old Singapore Sling area, which was removed for the 2023 race onward, simplifying that part of the lap and dropping the braking-zone count from 11 to 10 per lap. This is the calendar's clearest example of why the circuit reference table is keyed by configuration era rather than circuit name alone — treating pre- and post-2023 Marina Bay as identical would ignore a real, physical change to the track that a driver and car have to adapt to.

chunks.title: Marina Bay Singapore
chunks.text: Given the combination of extreme heat/humidity, a bumpy street surface, and a high safety-car rate, races here are among the least "position stays static" of any hard-to-overtake circuit — not because passing is easy, but because incidents and cautions reshuffle the order more than at almost any other track.

chunks.title: Melbourne
chunks.text:
Albert Park Circuit (Melbourne) — Circuit Notes
Albert Park is run on public roads around a park lake, which is why it's flagged as a street-type circuit in the reference table (is_street_circuit = 1), even though it's wider and more flowing than a tight downtown street track like Monaco or Baku. Since the circuit's significant 2022 reprofiling (walls pushed back, several corners widened and reshaped specifically to encourage racing), overtaking difficulty here sits at a genuinely moderate level (≈0.5) rather than the much harder rating the old, tighter layout would have earned — this is a good example of a circuit where a real physical change should shift how much weight grid position carries relative to older seasons at the same track.
Safety car frequency is moderate (≈0.5) — the lakeside walls are unforgiving if a car gets it wrong, but the reprofiled corners give more margin than before. DNF rate is a fairly typical ≈0.12. Tyre degradation is on the low side (≈2/5), consistent with a track that rewards a smooth, flowing driving style over one that punishes the tyres through sustained high-lateral-load corners.
As an early-season race (often the second or third round), Melbourne shares Bahrain's characteristic of reflecting pre-season and prior-year form more than mid-season in-year development trends.

chunks.title: Mexico City
chunks.text:
Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez (Mexico City) — Circuit Notes
Mexico City's defining physical characteristic isn't captured directly in the standard reference-table columns but shapes everything about how the circuit behaves: it sits at roughly 2,200m altitude, among the highest of any F1 venue, where thinner air reduces both aerodynamic downforce and engine power, and teams run cars with unusually high wing levels to compensate. This is part of why overtaking difficulty is moderate (≈0.45) despite a long back straight into the stadium section's hard-braking Turn 1 — cars carry more drag than usual, which both aids slipstreaming on the straight and costs pure top speed.
The circuit has one of the shorter pit-lane loss times outside Montréal (≈18s), and DNF rate and safety car frequency are both fairly average (≈0.1 and ≈0.4). Tyre degradation is on the lower side (≈2/5) — the reduced grip and load from thin air actually means less absolute stress on the tyres than the corner speeds alone would suggest at sea level.
The final stadium section, run through a packed grandstand inside the old baseball stadium, is one of the most atmospheric and overtaking-relevant parts of the lap — cars are close together and slow enough there for genuine wheel-to-wheel racing even without a formal DRS zone.

chunks.title: Miami
chunks.text:
Miami International Autodrome — Circuit Notes
Miami is a purpose-built temporary circuit around the Hard Rock Stadium campus — classified as a street circuit (is_street_circuit = 1) even though, like Melbourne, it's wider and more permanent-feeling than a genuine downtown street track. Overtaking difficulty is moderate (≈0.5): there's a long back straight into a hard-braking zone that creates a real passing opportunity, offset by several tighter, wall-lined sections earlier in the lap where a mistake is costly.
Safety car frequency is on the higher side (≈0.6), consistent with most temporary/street-adjacent circuits — walls close to the racing line mean incidents are more likely to require a full safety car rather than resolving themselves. DNF rate (≈0.12) and tyre degradation (≈3/5) are both fairly typical mid-pack values. Rain is a minor factor (≈0.05) given the race's typical early-May date and South Florida climate, though it is not negligible the way it is at the Gulf-region rounds.
As with Jeddah, being a newer temporary layout means track evolution across the weekend (rubber laid down, grip building session to session) is more pronounced than at a permanent circuit with a stable, long-established surface.

chunks.title: Monaco
chunks.text:
Circuit de Monaco — Circuit Notes
Monaco is the single hardest circuit on the calendar to overtake at (overtaking_difficulty ≈ 0.95, the highest value in the reference table by a clear margin) — the track is barely wider than the cars in several places, run through the streets of the Principality with barriers immediately off the racing line and essentially no realistic passing zone under green-flag racing. This is the canonical example of a circuit where grid position is close to destiny: a driver who qualifies well is very likely to finish close to where they started, and a driver who qualifies poorly has almost no way to recover through overtaking alone (track position gained via pit-stop strategy or a safety car becomes disproportionately valuable instead).
Because passing is so difficult, the track's tyre degradation is rated the lowest in the calendar (≈1/5) — cars aren't fighting for position lap after lap the way they do at an overtaking-friendly circuit, so tyre life is rarely the limiting factor in a Monaco strategy the way pure track position is. The circuit is also the shortest on the calendar (3.337 km), meaning more laps are needed to cover full race distance, which raises the cumulative chance that a red flag, safety car, or VSC period (safety_car_frequency ≈ 0.6) reshuffles the strategic picture at some point in the race.

chunks.title: Monaco
chunks.text: Monaco is the single clearest real-world illustration of why a model needs a grid-position-times-overtaking-difficulty interaction feature: the same grid position is worth far more here than at an easy-overtaking track like Monza.

chunks.title: Montreal
chunks.text:
Circuit Gilles Villeneuve (Montréal) — Circuit Notes
Montréal is a semi-permanent circuit on Île Notre-Dame, built around a mix of long straights and tight chicanes, with a famous wall at the final corner exit (the "Wall of Champions") that has ended more than one championship contender's race. It carries the shortest pit-lane loss time in the entire reference table (≈15.5s) — the pit lane here is unusually short relative to lap distance — which meaningfully changes the math on whether an extra pit stop is worth attempting compared to almost any other circuit on the calendar.
Overtaking difficulty is moderate (≈0.35), helped by long straights into hard-braking chicanes, but the circuit has the highest DNF rate in the reference table (≈0.2) and a high safety car frequency (≈0.8, second only to Marina Bay) — the combination of high speed, concrete walls very close to the racing line, and frequently changeable weather (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.2, one of the higher values outside of Spa/Silverstone/São Paulo) makes this one of the most unpredictable, caution-heavy rounds of the season.
Given the low pit-loss cost and high safety-car frequency, race-winning strategy at Montréal is disproportionately about being ready to react to a caution period rather than executing a pre-planned stint plan — a driver's realistic finishing position here is less "locked in" by qualifying than the raw overtaking-difficulty number alone would suggest.

chunks.title: Monza
chunks.text:
Autodromo Nazionale Monza — Circuit Notes
Monza is F1's classic "Temple of Speed" and has the lowest overtaking_difficulty rating in the entire reference table (≈0.2) — the layout is dominated by long straights (the front straight and the run through the Parabolica) into heavy-braking chicanes, which is about as favourable a geometry for passing as exists anywhere on the calendar. It also has the highest pit_lane_loss_time in the reference table (≈23s) — because lap times here are so short relative to other circuits, even a small pit-lane time loss represents a larger fraction of a lap than at a longer, slower circuit, which affects the undercut/overcut math.
Safety car frequency (≈0.2) and DNF rate (≈0.1) are both on the low side — Monza's chicanes are slow and forgiving by design, and its long straights don't carry the same wall-proximity risk as a street circuit at similar speed. Tyre degradation is comparatively low (≈2/5), since much of the lap is flat-out running rather than sustained cornering load.
Monza is the natural opposite pole to Monaco/Hungaroring/Zandvoort in any circuit-interaction analysis: grid position should matter comparatively little here, and a model that shows `grid_x_overtaking_difficulty` mattering far less at Monza than at those tracks is behaving exactly as the underlying racing reality suggests it should.

chunks.title: Sao Paulo Interlagos
chunks.text:
Autódromo José Carlos Pace (Interlagos, São Paulo) — Circuit Notes
Interlagos is a short, anti-clockwise permanent circuit (one of the few anti-clockwise tracks on the calendar, which creates unusual neck-load demands compared to most other rounds) with significant elevation change across the lap. Overtaking difficulty is on the easier side (≈0.3) — the start/finish straight into Turn 1 (the Senna S) is one of the most reliable overtaking spots in Formula 1, helped by the long uphill approach that makes slipstreaming effective.
Rain is a major factor here (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.35, tied with Spa for one of the highest in the reference table) — São Paulo's local climate produces sudden, intense tropical storms, and mixed or fully wet Interlagos races (including several famous title-deciding ones) are a recurring feature of the calendar rather than an exception. Safety car frequency (≈0.4) and DNF rate (≈0.12) are both moderately elevated, consistent with a short, technical lap where a rain-affected session compounds the normal risk of the technical Senna S and Turn 1 braking zone.
Given the combination of easy overtaking and frequent rain, Interlagos is one of the calendar's least "grid position is destiny" circuits — both the layout and the weather independently push toward more mixed-up, less predictable finishing orders than the average round.

chunks.title: Sepang Kuala Lumpur
chunks.text:
Sepang International Circuit, near Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Track length 5.543 km, 15 corners, 56 race laps. Formula 1 raced here as the Malaysian Grand Prix from 1999 to 2017; in 2026 it returns to host the Bahrain Grand Prix. None of this project's 2022-2026 data comes from Sepang, so every circuit value for it is an estimate from the layout and its earlier history, and should be revisited once a race has run.
Overtaking is relatively easy (difficulty ≈0.35): two long straights, the start-finish straight and the back straight, each end in heavy braking into a slow corner (Turn 1 and the Turn 15 hairpin), and the back straight into Turn 15 is the classic passing place. Cars can follow through the fast sweepers of the first sector less well.
Tyre degradation is high (≈4 on the 1-5 scale): an abrasive surface, long high-speed corners and track temperatures often above 50°C wear tyres quickly, which historically made two-stop races common.
Weather is the big unknown. Afternoon tropical thunderstorms are frequent (rain chance ≈0.35 in the reference table), heat and humidity make it one of the most physically demanding races for drivers, and the heat stresses brakes and power units, which is why its retirement rate is estimated above average (≈0.15). Safety cars have been moderately common (≈0.4), often weather-related.

chunks.title: Shanghai
chunks.text:
Shanghai International Circuit — Circuit Notes
Shanghai is a large, purpose-built permanent circuit distinguished by an unusually long, decreasing-radius Turn 1-2-3 complex (often compared to a snail shell) and one of the longest back straights on the calendar (≈1,170m) into a hard-braking hairpin. That combination keeps overtaking_difficulty at a moderate level (≈0.4) — the back straight is a genuine, reliable passing zone, similar in character to Austin or Bahrain.
Pit-lane loss time is on the higher side (≈22s), and tyre degradation is moderate (≈3/5) — the long, high-speed corners of the opening complex put real sustained load through the tyres despite the circuit's otherwise fairly conventional layout. Rain is a real if secondary factor (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.15), consistent with Shanghai's typically damp spring race date. Safety car frequency (≈0.4) and DNF rate (≈0.1) are both close to the calendar median.
Shanghai's return to the calendar after a multi-year absence (following construction and pandemic-era cancellations) means its more recent rows carry less accumulated recent track-form history for some drivers than a circuit that's been raced every year without interruption — worth remembering when a driver's `driver_track_form` value at this circuit looks unusually sparse.

chunks.title: Silverstone
chunks.text:
Silverstone Circuit — Circuit Notes
Silverstone is one of the fastest permanent circuits on the calendar, built on a former WWII airfield, with a sequence of high-speed corners (Maggotts, Becketts, Chapel) that are among the most demanding in Formula 1. Despite that speed, overtaking difficulty is on the lower side (≈0.35) — the long Hangar Straight into the Stowe/Vale braking zone, plus the Wellington Straight, both create real passing opportunities that offset the technical middle sector.
Tyre degradation is rated at the top of the scale (≈4/5, tied with Bahrain/Barcelona/Spa/Suzuka) — the sustained high-speed lateral loading through Maggotts-Becketts-Chapel is some of the hardest cornering load tyres see anywhere on the calendar. Silverstone also has the highest rain_race_frequency among the "permanent circuit" group (≈0.25) — British summer weather is famously unpredictable, and a wet or mixed-conditions Silverstone race is a regular occurrence rather than a rare event, which is part of why practice and qualifying pace here can be a noisier predictor of race-day pace than at a more climatically stable venue.
Safety car frequency (≈0.3) and DNF rate (≈0.1) are both moderate — the circuit has generous, modern run-off in most places, but the sheer cornering speed means the corners that do punish a mistake tend to do so decisively.

chunks.title: Spa
chunks.text:
Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps — Circuit Notes
Spa is the longest circuit on the F1 calendar (7.004 km) and, alongside Bahrain, has the lowest overtaking_difficulty rating in the reference table (≈0.25) — the run from Eau Rouge/Raidillon up the Kemmel Straight into the Les Combes braking zone is one of the most famous and reliable overtaking opportunities in motorsport, and the long lap also means multiple further passing zones elsewhere. This is a track where a poor qualifying result is one of the most recoverable in the whole calendar.
Spa has the highest rain_race_frequency of any circuit in the reference table (≈0.35) — the Ardennes forest region is famous for its own microclimate, where it can be raining at one part of the circuit and dry at another within the same lap, which is a genuinely unique strategic challenge (mixed-conditions tyre choice) that few other circuits present at this scale. Tyre degradation is rated high (≈3/5, and effectively higher in practice given the very high average speed and long straights that load tyres differently than a technical circuit). Safety car frequency (≈0.5) and DNF rate (≈0.12) are both elevated by the combination of high average speed and a track that, despite modern run-off at Eau Rouge, still punishes a mistake at the wrong moment severely.

chunks.title: Spa
chunks.text: Spa is a strong counter-example to Monaco/Hungaroring/Zandvoort in any circuit-interaction SHAP analysis — grid position should matter comparatively little here relative to those tracks, precisely because overtaking is genuinely easy.

chunks.title: Spielberg
chunks.text:
Red Bull Ring (Spielberg) — Circuit Notes
The Red Bull Ring is one of the shortest permanent lap distances on the calendar (4.318 km) set in the Styrian hills, with dramatic elevation change and just three real braking zones per lap (the lowest braking-zone count in the reference table) — most of the circuit is flowing, high-speed corners connected by short straights. That layout keeps overtaking difficulty moderate (≈0.4): the three hard-braking zones are all genuine passing opportunities, but there's comparatively little of the lap where a pass can actually be attempted.
Tyre degradation is on the higher side (≈3/5) for a circuit this short, since the fast, sweeping corners put sustained load through the tyres despite the low overall lap distance. Safety car frequency (≈0.3) and DNF rate (≈0.1) are both fairly average, and rain is a moderate factor (≈0.1) given the circuit's mountainous setting, where weather can change quickly within a race weekend.
Because the lap is so short, drivers spend a larger fraction of total race distance in genuinely high-speed, low-margin-for-error corners than at a longer circuit — small qualifying-pace deficits tend to compound less dramatically over a race distance here than at a circuit with more low-speed technical sections to lose time in.

chunks.title: Suzuka
chunks.text:
Suzuka International Racing Course — Circuit Notes
Suzuka is one of the most technically demanding circuits on the calendar, famous for its figure-eight layout (the only crossover circuit in F1) and the high-speed Esses/130R sequence. Overtaking difficulty sits at a moderate level (≈0.5) — the hairpin and the final chicane both offer real passing chances, but the flowing middle sector is unforgiving of a car that isn't fundamentally quick, so grid position still carries meaningful weight even where a pass is technically possible.
Tyre degradation is rated at the top of the scale (≈4/5) — the sustained high-speed direction changes through the Esses put some of the highest lateral load on tyres anywhere on the calendar. Rain is a significant factor (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.3) given Suzuka's typical autumn date and Japan's typhoon-season weather patterns — wet-weather Suzuka races, including red-flagged sessions, are a recurring feature of the calendar rather than a rare event.
Safety car frequency (≈0.3) and DNF rate (≈0.1) are both moderate, reflecting a circuit that rewards precision and punishes a lack of it, without being as consistently incident-prone as a street circuit. Suzuka's combination of high degradation and moderate overtaking difficulty makes tyre strategy and pit-stop timing a particularly important explanatory factor here relative to pure grid position.

chunks.title: Yas Island Abudhabi
chunks.text:
Yas Marina Circuit (Yas Island, Abu Dhabi) — Circuit Notes
Yas Marina hosts the traditional season finale and underwent a significant 2021 reprofiling (several corners in the final sector were reshaped and widened specifically to improve overtaking, after the circuit had developed a reputation as one of the hardest to pass at on the calendar). Since that change, overtaking_difficulty is rated at a moderate level (≈0.55) — a meaningful improvement on the old layout's reputation, though still tighter than a genuine power circuit like Monza or Bahrain.
DNF rate is among the lowest in the reference table (≈0.08) — the circuit has generous, modern run-off throughout, and by the time of the season finale, most reliability issues that are going to surface across a season have typically already done so on cars that make it this far. Safety car frequency (≈0.3) and tyre degradation (≈2/5) are both moderate, and rain is a non-factor given the UAE desert climate (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.0).
Being the final round of the season means this circuit's rows often carry extra significance for championship-outcome context even though the reference table itself only captures track characteristics — a driver's recent form and season-long track-form features going into Abu Dhabi reflect a full season's accumulated data, more than at any earlier round.

chunks.title: Zandvoort
chunks.text:
Circuit Zandvoort — Circuit Notes
Zandvoort returned to the F1 calendar in 2021 after a long absence, reconfigured with banked corners (most notably the final corner) inspired by American oval racing, in an attempt to improve overtaking at what is fundamentally a narrow, dune-constrained old-school circuit. Despite the banking, overtaking_difficulty is rated the second-highest in the entire reference table (≈0.85, behind only Monaco) — the track is simply too narrow through most of its lap for the banking alone to fix the underlying passing problem, and the circuit has few genuine straight-into-hard-braking zones.
Tyre degradation is moderate (≈3/5), and rain is a real factor given the North Sea coastal location (rain_race_frequency ≈ 0.15) — Dutch coastal weather can turn quickly, and the dunes that give the circuit its character also create localized wind effects that can catch drivers out. Safety car frequency is moderate (≈0.4), broadly in line with other narrow permanent circuits with limited run-off in key corners.
Given how close Zandvoort's overtaking difficulty sits to Monaco's, a well-tuned model should show grid position and grid-times-overtaking-difficulty interaction features carrying similarly outsized weight at both — Zandvoort is a useful check on whether a circuit-aware feature is really learning "hard to pass" rather than just memorizing "this is Monaco."
